passage: After failing his first programming project at university in Osaka, Hiroshi stopped opening his laptop for anything but videos. "I'm just not a coder," he told Astrid. In November he tried something smaller. Every evening he solved one tiny problem: reverse a word, count the vowels in a sentence, find the biggest number in a list. Each took ten or twenty minutes. He wrote each one in a small green notebook with the date. By January the notebook had fifty-three entries. One night he flipped back and laughed at problem three, which had taken him an hour. Now he'd do it in two minutes. He showed Astrid. "Fifty-three," she read. "So you are a coder." That weekend he started rebuilding the project he had failed.

Dear Uday,
Remember how I cried on the phone after my internship coding test in June? I really thought I'd picked the wrong degree.
Here's what I've been doing since. Every morning before class, I solve one small coding problem, the tiniest ones on the practice site, like "reverse a string" or "check if a number is prime". Then I log it in a spreadsheet: date, problem, how long it took. Yesterday I hit row 100. 🎉
I scrolled back to row 1. It took me 45 minutes to reverse a string. Now I'd do it in five. I never noticed getting better day by day, but the list doesn't lie.
I've signed up for the next internship test in March. Still nervous. But less.
Love,
Pallavi didi

The spring after I failed my first programming course, I avoided my laptop like a hot stove. I'm Alka. I'd been the top student in school maths, and now I couldn't make a simple function run.
My hostel senior Shalini told me what she'd done: “Solve one small problem a day. Only one. Then log it.”
I started a spreadsheet. Row 1: print a pattern of stars. Row 2: add two numbers entered by a user. Silly things.
Some days took five minutes, some took an hour. But I didn't skip a day.
At row 40, I scrolled back to the top. Row 1 looked so easy now. That was the moment I believed I could actually learn this.
I passed the re-exam in autumn. The spreadsheet has 212 rows now. I still add one most nights.

Lab mentor's note, computer science, by Charu
Yogesh failed the programming practical in the second semester and since then has avoided the lab. Last month he told me, "I'm not a coder. I should switch branches."
I suggested an experiment: one tiny problem a day, fifteen minutes, from the beginner list, and write each one he solved in a notebook with the date.
Today he showed me the notebook. Twenty-six problems. Reverse a string. Count vowels. Find the largest number. Small things. But he read them out slowly, and I could see his shoulders lift with each line.
"I did all of these?" he asked.
"Every one."
What I did next: I gave him a problem from the intermediate list for this week, and asked him to come to lab hours on Friday to try it with me. He said yes before I finished the sentence.

After she failed the first programming test at the polytechnic in Hassan, Chandrika stopped opening the lab computer unless she had to. "Coding isn't for people like me," she told Pranav at the tea stall by the bus stand.
Pranav didn't argue. He tore a page from his notebook. "One tiny problem a day. Ten minutes. Reverse a word, add two numbers, anything. Write it here when it works."

On the day of the retest, waiting outside the lab, she ran her finger down the list. Twenty-six things that worked. She went in.
